title: The Zα domain of ADAR1: emerging roles in cancer biology and evidence as a promising therapeutic target

paragraphs.en: Adenosine deaminase acting on RNA 1 (ADAR1) is an RNA editing enzyme that catalyzes the deamination of adenosine, converting it to inosine. This type of adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) editing occurs primarily within Alu-rich double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), thereby preventing aberrant activation of innate immune sensing of endogenous dsRNA. 1 , 2 Dysregulated ADAR1 editing activity has been linked to cancer cell fitness, immune evasion and therapy resistance across multiple cancer types, including breast, liver, esophageal, colorectal, lung, and head and neck cancers. 3-7 The majority of the published work emphasized ADAR1's RNA editing function as the dominant mechanism by which ADAR1 promotes tumor growth and immune escape. These aspects are well covered in recent reviews and remain fundamental. 8‐11 Yet, in more recent years, editing-independent functions mediated through other domains of ADAR1 have also moved to the foreground. Several recent reviews have begun to discuss more comprehensively, both editing-dependent and editing-independent roles of ADAR1 in cancer biology. 12 , 13

Importantly, ADAR1 exists as two major isoforms: the constitutive, predominantly nuclear p110 isoform and the interferon (IFN)-inducible, predominantly cytoplasmic p150 isoform. Large-scale genome-wide shRNA and CRISPR/Cas9 screening datasets, such as the Project DRIVE 14 and Cancer Dependency Map, 15 as well as independent loss-of-function studies, have repeatedly identified ADAR1 as a cancer dependency enriched in IFN-high contexts. 16‐19 Through our own functional genomic work in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), we provided strong evidence that the IFN can sensitize non-dependent OSCC to the loss of ADAR1, while the expression of the ADAR1-p150 (but not p110) can potently reverse the ADAR1 knockout-induced lethality phenotype. 17 This provides a strong rationale for targeting the IFN-inducible p150 isoform as an effective and specific therapeutic approach in ADAR1-dependent cancers. 17 , 20 In support of this, isoform resolved analyses demonstrated that p150 edits a broader and distinct set of RNA substrates 21 and occupies distinct interaction networks compared with p110, 20 despite sharing an identical deaminase domain. This suggests that both isoforms impact transcription in their unique ways.

Beyond subcellular localization, ADAR1-p150 is further distinguished from p110 by the presence of an additional N-terminal Zα domain that binds left-handed Z-DNA and Z-RNA (collectively referred to as Z-nucleic acids, ZNAs). 22 Our earlier work has demonstrated that the Zα domain of the ADAR1-p150 is required for its localization to the cytoplasmic stress granules. 23 Notably, this Zα domain is found in only one other protein among mammals, the Z-DNA-binding protein 1 (ZBP1). Defects in the ADAR1 Zα–ZNA axis unleash ZBP1-driven inflammatory signaling and/or regulated cell death programs. 24‐26 These three studies published in Nature demonstrated that ZBP1 acts as a key effector of immunopathology when ADAR1 Zα function is impaired, thereby establishing ZNAs sensing as biologically consequential and partially independent of canonical necroptosis pathways. 24 , 26 Concurrent structural, biochemical and mutagenesis studies have further refined ADAR1 domain architecture and enzymology, informing drug discovery efforts and suggesting that Zα-dependent functions extend beyond RNA editing per se. 27 , 28

Translational momentum in the field is rapidly increasing. In recent years, studies and pharmaceutical/biotechnology companies have disclosed small molecule ADAR1 inhibitors, including compounds and degraders with selectivity towards the Zα domain and/or the p150 isoform. 29‐33 Despite the rich literature on ADAR1's RNA editing activity and growing translational interest in targeting ADAR1 for cancer therapy and immunotherapy combination, there remains a lack of focused review on the Zα domain itself and its unique contribution to p150-mediated tumor cell survival and immune modulation. 22 , 34 , 35

To address this gap, herein this review, we discuss the role of the ADAR1-p150's Zα domain in cancer biology and emerging therapeutic opportunities. Given the foundational role of the Zα domain in nucleic acid binding, we first describe the structural and biochemical interactions between the ZNAs and the Zα domain. We discuss recent understanding on the emerging roles of ZNAs in driving tumorigenesis and the therapeutic strategies targeting the Zα domain to block the ZNA-Zα interactions. Center to this, we present the current methodologies enabling the detection and analyses of ZNA-Zα interactions. Finally, we outline key challenges in ZNA-Zα research and conclude with future perspectives on the translational cancer biology aspects of ADAR1 and its Zα domain.

sections.title: Z-nucleic acids (ZNAs) and the Zα domain in ADAR1

paragraphs.en: Typically, nucleic acids in cells adopt right-handed helical conformations, with B-DNA representing the canonical form of DNA and A-like geometry commonly observed for dsRNA. This understanding was expanded with the discovery of Z-DNA through crystallographic studies by Alexander Rich and colleagues. 36 They demonstrated that unlike B-DNA, Z-DNA adopts a left-handed conformation with a characteristic zig-zag phosphate backbone. They further showed that alternating purine-pyrimidine sequences, particularly CG repeats, have a higher tendency to form this Z-conformation (Figure 1A). 37 Early biophysical studies suggested that Z-DNA is usually transient, as it requires high energy and specific conditions to form. 37 In vitro, high salt concentrations such as 3–4 M NaCl are required to stabilize the Z-conformation. 36 , 38 Negative supercoiling generated during transcription and chemical modifications such as cytosine methylation were later shown to promote the B-to-Z transition, allowing for Z-DNA formation under more physiological relevant conditions. 39‐42 These findings shifted the perception on Z-DNA from a ligand that has limited biological relevance to biologically meaningful molecule. 43‐46 The Z-prone sequences in the genome, termed as Z-flipons are unlocking many new insights into previously unresolved biology, as discussed in several recent reviews. 22 , 47 , 48

This discovery of the ADAR1-p150's unique Zα domain provided the first evidence that ADAR1-p150 could sense and selectively bind to Z-DNA. 49 Subsequent identification of similar domain in ZBP1 and in viral proteins, established Z-DNA recognition as an evolutionarily conserved biological mechanism. 13,50‐52 Although initially characterized as a Z-DNA binding domain, subsequent work demonstrated that dsRNA can also adopt similar Z-conformation and hence named Z-RNA. While Zα binds both forms of ZNAs with comparable affinity, Z‑RNA forms kinetically more stable complexes with Zα. 53 The observation that Zα domains bind ZNAs but fail to recognize identical sequences in their canonical forms demonstrates that Zα binding is not sequence-specific, but instead depends on the adoption of the Z-conformation. 54‐57 The discovery of Z-RNA binding redefined Zα from merely a Z-DNA binder to RNA-structure sensor. This insight is particularly relevant for ADAR1 as an RNA-editing enzyme because Zα is found only in the IFN-inducible p150 isoform, which is mainly cytoplasmic (though capable of nuclear shuttling), and not in the nuclear p110 isoform. 58 , 59 Such localization places ADAR1-p150 in proximity to endogenousdsRNA species arising from repetitive elements, inverted Alu pairs and other structured transcripts, thereby providing a plausible spatial context for Z-RNA sensing (Figure 1C). In this setting, the Zα domain may help p150 engage, position or regulate structurally unusual RNA substrates in ways that influence not only RNA editing, but also editing-independent control of RNA sensing and innate immune activation. 60 , 61

Structurally, ADAR1-p150's Zα adopts a winged helix–turn–helix fold which consists of three α-helices packed against a small β-sheet. This pre-formed binding surface interacts with the zig-zag backbone of ZNAs through a network of electrostatic and hydrogen-bonding interactions (Figure 1B). 37 , 54 , 55 , 62 Within ADAR1-p150 Zα, there are several conserved residues, namely N173, Y177, P193 and W195 which are collectively central to ZNAs binding, recognition and structural integrity, which hold translational relevance. 54 , 63 Within α3 helix, N173 is key to high-affinity nucleic acid binding, as it is pre‑organized in the orientation that favor ADAR1-p150 to engage Z‑RNA efficiently. N173A mutation markedly reduces binding affinity and the N173S variant is linked to Aicardi–Goutières syndrome (AGS). 64 On the other hand, Y177 helps distinguish between RNA and DNA and also contributes to the recognition of the Z‑form over B-form nucleic acid. 54 , 62 Within the β-sheet, P193 helps maintain the structural architecture by restricting loop flexibility and ensuring proper positioning of the recognition surface. Clinically, P193A mutation is often observed in patients with AGS and bilateral striatal necrosis. 65 W195 helps stabilise the structural scaffold of Zα and is required for effective Z-RNA recognition. W195A (W197A in mouse) mutation disrupts Z-RNA binding and causes massive degradation of the protein inside the cell which results in AGS-like inflammatory phenotypes in vivo. 66 Collectively, these key residues provide a rational structural basis for the development of Zα-targeting drugs. Although limited, early virtual screening and binding-based studies support the tractability of this domain as a pharmacological target, reinforcing its emerging relevance in isoform-selective ADAR1-p150 targeting strategies. 29‐31,67‐69

Taken together, structural and biophysical studies of the ADAR1-p150's Zα domain have established a framework for our understanding on ZNAs binding interactions. This structural capability provides an important foundation for the reported biological roles of ADAR1 Zα in regulating RNA sensing pathways and innate immune responses. 70 , 71

sections.title: Cellular functions of the ADAR1-p150's Zα domain and its emerging role in cancer biology

paragraphs.en: Through the structural recognition of ZNAs, the ADAR1-p150's Zα domain plays critical roles in regulating fundamental cellular processes. Mutations in Zα abolish Z-RNA binding and reduce editing of subsets of endogenous RNAs, particularly within the repetitive elements in the 3′ untranslated region (3′UTR). 66 , 72 Consistently, dsRNA substrates containing Z-form–prone sequences exhibit enhanced A-to-I editing efficiency (~40%), compared to non–Z-forming substrates (8%). 73 Given that the Zα domain lacks catalytic activity, its effects on RNA editing are likely indirect, with Z-RNA binding promoting substrate recognition and positioning of the RNA molecule for editing by ADAR1-p150's deaminase domain. Transcriptome-wide analyses such as CLIP-seq and RIP-seq, further demonstrates ADAR1 Zα interactions extend beyond Alu elements to 3′UTRs and primary microRNA transcripts, implicating Zα-mediated recognition in post-transcriptional regulation and oncogenic pathways. 74 , 75 However, little is known about the specific editing sites or genes affected by ADAR1–Zα–ZNA interactions, as site-specific changes are generally modest in studies of Zα mutations. 76‐78

Z-DNA, encoded by flipons can arise under physiological conditions associated with transcriptional stress and has been linked to genomic instability, likely through aberrant engagement of DNA repair processes, implicating their role in cancer biology. 79‐83 Although the precise contribution of Zα to RNA editing in cancer remains unclear, the ADAR1-p150 which uniquely contains Zα is increasingly recognized as a key driver of tumor cell survival, partially through its deaminase activity. 17 ZNAs may facilitate substrate targeting for deamination, thereby linking structural sensing to RNA editing and contributing to oncogenic mechanisms in solid tumors. 17 , 84 , 85

The ADAR1-p150 isoform edits endogenous dsRNA to prevent recognition by innate sensors, suppressing Melanoma Differentiation-Associated protein 5 (MDA5)-mediated type I IFN signaling, Protein kinase R (PKR)-induced translational shutdown and apoptosis. 1 , 71 , 86 , 87 The loss of ADAR1 leads to suppression of tumor growth and enhancement of anti-tumor immunity. 19 , 88 , 89 By dampening these sensing pathways, ADAR1-p150 promotes tumor cell survival, immune tolerance, and resistance to immune checkpoint blockade in cancers with high-IFN signatures. 19 , 88 , 89 Other than PKR and MDA5, ZBP1 is another key sensor regulating inflammatory cell death. Several studies have shown that mutations in the ADAR1-p150's Zα domain, such as W197A and P195A disrupt Z-RNA recognition in mice, leading to dsRNA accumulation and upregulation of IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs) via the MDA5/MAVS pathway. 66 , 90 These observations suggest that disrupting Z-RNA recognition by the Zα domain can enhance ISG induction via the sensing pathway. Consistently, minimal ISG upregulation was observed in Human Embryonic Kidney (HEK) cells with equivalent mutations, due to lack of dsRNA sensor (MDA5) expression. 91 This further indicates that the response depends on the availability of sensing machinery, highlighting the link between Zα-mediated RNA recognition and innate immune activation.

Besides, the Zα domain is required to suppress spontaneous ZBP1 activation and the associated cell death mechanism. Generally, two mechanisms have been proposed. Firstly, in ADAR1-deficient mice, loss of Zα-mediated A-to-I editing of endogenous Alu elements permits the formation of dsRNA duplexes from inverted Alu repeats, which can activate ZBP1. 25 This led to ZBP1-driven caspase-8–dependent apoptosis and MLKL-mediated necroptosis, contributing to embryonic lethality and tissue inflammation. 25 Consistently, ADAR1 Zα mutations promote ZBP1 signaling through RIPK3 and caspase-8, leading to inflammatory cell death and overt disease phenotypes. Notably, these phenotypes are reversed when ZBP1 is ablated. 24 Secondly, ADAR1-p150 is proposed to directly interact with ZBP1 through their respective Zα domain, inhibiting ZBP1 activation. 71 Using nuclear export inhibitor to sequester ADAR1-p150 in the nucleus could prevent its interaction with ZNAs in the cytoplasm, thereby allowing ZNA sensing by ZBP1 and inducing PANoptosis. Together, these findings establish that the ADAR1-p150's Zα domain is a critical negative regulator of ZBP1, preventing endogenous ZNA-mediated activation of inflammatory cell death and pathological immune signaling.

The Zα domain of ADAR1-p150 is essential for the localization of ADAR1-p150 protein to cytoplasmic stress granules through ZNAs binding. 23 Stress granules are cytoplasmic foci triggered by cellular stresses, such as hypoxia, nutrient deprivation, oxidative stress, and immune responses—typical challenges in tumor microenvironment. 92‐95 In addition, chemoresistance has been associated with stress granules formation. 96 , 97 The function of ADAR1-p150 within stress granules is currently a subject of diligent research. The condensed architecture of stress granules could stabilize the formation of ZNAs, otherwise energetically unfavourable. 98 The ZNAs binding by the Zα domain of ADAR1-p150 may promote unique associations within stress granules, altering editing specificity and protein-protein interactions. Several cancer cell line studies have linked ADAR1-p150 to stress granules. For example, in HeLa cells, it colocalizes with core stress granule markers under conditions such as arsenite treatment or transfection with long dsRNA. Under these conditions, ADAR1-p150 recruitment to stress granules is thought to support cell survival, potentially by editing a subset of sequestered RNAs to generate inosine-containing dsRNA (IU-dsRNA), thereby suppressing apoptosis and excessive ISG induction. 99 Using A549 and U2OS cells as the study models, ADAR1-p150 also acts as a negative regulator of stress granule formation through both PKR-dependent mechanisms, by suppressing dsRNA-mediated PKR activation and preserving translation, and PKR-independent mechanisms, by limiting RNA–RNA and RNA–protein interactions required for granule assembly. 100 Together, these findings indicate that ADAR1-p150 is recruited to stress granules under cellular stress, where it contributes to cell survival while also modulating stress granule assembly through multiple regulatory mechanisms. The link of these mechanisms to cancer dependency on the ADAR1's Zα domain remain to be further investigated.

Collectively, these studies highlight the role of ADAR1-p150's Zα in sensing ZNAs, regulating RNA editing, restraining inflammatory pathways, and promoting tumor stress tolerance. Given the reliance on ADAR1-p150 for cancer cells survival, this positions the Zα domain as a promising therapeutic target, where selective inhibition of its ZNAs recognition capability could disrupt cancer cells survival mechanisms and enhance anti-tumor immunity. Targeting ADAR1-p150's Zα is therefore an innovative strategy to both suppress tumor growth and sensitize cancers to immune checkpoint blockade.

The growing evidence of ADAR1 in regulating innate immune suppression in AGS and cancer has driven interest in translating these biological findings into therapeutic strategies. 1 , 60 , 88 , 101 , 102 A structured literature search was conducted in PubMed for articles published up to 28th February 2026. Searches combined target-related terms (“ADAR1”, “ADAR1-p150”, “ADAR1-p110”, “Zα”, “Z-DNA”, “Z-RNA” and “Z-nucleic acid”) with therapeutic and drug-discovery terms including “inhibitor”, “binder”, “degrader”, “PROTAC”, “drug discovery”, “virtual screening”, “splice modulator”, “nuclear export” and “RNA editing inhibitor”. Additional compound-specific searches and backward and forward citation tracking of relevant studies were performed to identify additional therapeutic strategies and subsequent validation or re-evaluation of reported compounds. Primary research articles were included if they provided experimental or mechanistic evidence relevant to therapeutic targeting of ADAR1, ADAR1-p150, the Zα domain or the broader ZNA sensing pathway. Secondary literature, including review articles, commentaries, editorials, conference abstracts, posters, and non-peer-reviewed reports, was excluded from the primary evidence synthesis. Reference lists of relevant reviews were manually examined and forward citation tracking was performed to ensure comprehensive coverage of the literature. Studies lacking direct evaluation of therapeutic interventions to ADAR1-, p150-, Zα-, or ZNA-related pathways were also excluded. Following screening, sixteen primary research articles were identified as relevant to the therapeutic targeting of the ADAR1 axis and are reviewed below.

Initial therapeutic approaches targeting ADAR1 have centered on inhibiting its catalytic A-to-I RNA editing activity. Earlier studies suggested that 8‑azaadenosine, 103 , 104 8‑chloroadenosine 105 and ZYS‑1 106 inhibited ADAR1 activity, which sparked excitement and triggered follow-up studies. However, these compounds were later clarified as not ADAR1-selective due to methodological errors and an oversight regarding ADAR1's dsRNA substrate specificity in the original experimental designs. 107 , 108 This reassessment helped establish more rigorous experimental standards for evaluating ADAR1 inhibition and alongside sharpened understanding of ADAR1 biology.

Continued efforts have since produced more refined catalytic inhibitors such as nucleoside analogs compound C12 33 and ADAR1i-124 109 (Figure 2-A1). These approaches provide proof-of-concept that pharmacological disruption of ADAR1 can phenocopy genetic loss and restore immune activation in tumor models, but their therapeutic potential remains constrained by limited isoform selectivity. Because the deaminase domain is shared by both p110 and p150, catalytic inhibitors are expected to act on both isoforms, raising concern that essential p110-dependent homeostatic functions may also be affected. Indeed, complete loss of ADAR1 results in embryonic lethality with widespread apoptosis, liver disintegration, and failure of hematopoietic stem-cell maintenance. 60 , 110 , 111 Isoform-specific studies further reveal that p150 deficiency drives MDA5/MAVS-dependent embryonic lethality and p110 loss leads to high postnatal mortality, highlighting their non-redundant and essential physiological roles. 60 , 112 , 113 Consistent with this, mechanistic studies show that ADAR1-p110 contributes to genome stability through the resolution of RNA:DNA hybrids (R-loops), with its depletion leading to telomeric R-loop accumulation and DNA damage, 114 collectively indicating that indiscriminate ADAR1 inhibition may carry inherent safety risks. As an example, ADAR1i-124 was reportedly causing an “unexpected” activation of PKR and subsequently, translational shutdown in ADAR1-p110 high glioblastoma cells, but not in ADAR1-p150 high melanoma cells. This observation unveils the risk of indiscriminate catalytic inhibition, which may trigger broad RNA stress responses beyond the intended therapeutic effect. Notably, the relative safety profile reported for ADAR1i-124 has been attributed to preservation of dsRNA-binding and other non-catalytic scaffolding functions. This suggests that retaining ADAR1 structure can mitigate some of the undesirable consequences associated with broader inhibition. Building on this idea, strategies that spare the entire ADAR1-p110 isoform while selectively targeting ADAR1-p150 may offer a safer therapeutic profile. While ADAR1i-124 demonstrated a favorable safety profile in glioblastoma and melanoma cells in vitro in short period, preclinical evaluation of ADAR1i-124 in vivo that could reveal long-term consequences of sustained p110 inhibition remained to be reported. 109 On the other hand, while C12 has shown preclinical efficacy and tolerable safety profile in prostate cancer xenograft models, further optimization of half-life is needed to improve therapeutic practicality. 33 Beyond catalytic inhibition, proximity-induced modalities such as Z-DNA-based Proteolysis Targeting Chimera (Z-PROTAC) have been explored to achieve targeted proteasomal degradation of ADAR1 (Figure 2-A2). Utilizing Z-DNA-binding ligands as targeting groups, these chimeras (e.g., variants 7c–9c) engage the shared Z-DNA-binding motifs, specifically the Zβ domain present in both isoforms and the Zα domain unique to p150, thereby directing ADAR1 for degradation. Their activity has thus far been demonstrated in vitro in multiple cancer cell models, including breast cancer, melanoma, and colorectal cancer cell lines, where Z-PROTAC-mediated ADAR1 depletion induced cell death and activated PANoptotic pathways. 32 While this approach does not fully discriminate between p110 and p150, it provides a high degree of protein-level specificity, sparing other Z-binding proteins such as ZBP1 and avoiding the off-target effects typical of nucleoside analogs. This complete degradation addresses the critical scaffolding functions of ADAR1, although it retains potential limitations associated with global loss of p110-mediated RNA editing. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that ADAR1 is highly druggable in a multi-pronged manner, but also underscore the need for selective and isoform-targeted approaches.

ADAR1-p150 has been identified as the dominant isoform responsible for A-to-I RNA editing, preferentially targeting 3′ UTR regions of mRNAs, due to its localization in the cytoplasm. This editing activity by ADAR1-p150 is sufficient to prevent the activation of PKR and MDA5 during IFN signaling, thereby suppressing lethal auto-immunity and maintaining cellular homeostasis. 21 , 60 , 76 , 111 , 113 Among current strategies, Rebecsinib employs the isoform-selective mechanism (Figure 2-B1). Rebecsinib is a splice-modulating agent that specifically attenuates ADAR1-p150 expression thereby limiting p150-dependent cytoplasmic RNA editing. In leukemia cells, Rebecsinib restores innate immune sensing and disrupts leukemia stem cell maintenance while preserving ADAR1-p110 activity in maintaining homeostasis. Its efficacy was subsequently tested in humanized leukemia mouse models. 115 Importantly, Rebecsinib has now progressed beyond preclinical evaluation, with a first-in-human Phase 1 trial of Rebecsinib (NCT07250646) currently recruiting patients with relapsed/refractory secondary acute myeloid leukemia or high-risk myelofibrosis. This study represents an important step towards the clinical translation of ADAR1-targeted therapies. The N-terminus of ADAR1-p150 contains a nuclear export signal that allows the protein to shuttle to the cytoplasm, where it inhibits ZBP1-mediated signalling. By preventing ADAR1-p150 from entering the cytoplasm, nuclear export inhibitors such as Selinexor (KPT-330) and Eltanexor (KPT-8602) have been shown to perturb ADAR1-p150-associated ZBP1 regulation and activate PANoptotic pathways in cell-based melanoma and immune-cell models. Their therapeutic effects were further supported in preclinical melanoma tumor models, particularly in combination with IFNs, where nuclear export inhibition increased tumor cell death and reduced tumor volume (Figure 2-B2). 71 , 116 However, because these agents broadly inhibit XPO1-mediated nuclear export, their effects are not specific to ADAR1-p150 and likely involve additional cellular pathways beyond ADAR1 regulation. Together, these approaches demonstrate that selective interference with ADAR1-p150 is feasible and therapeutically meaningful. This therefore represents a critical gap where more specific and selective inhibition of the Zα domain is warranted. Given that AGS-associated Zα mutations, like N173S and P193A (P195A in mouse), are sufficient to trigger an immune response even when the catalytic domain remains intact. 61 , 64 , 65 This genetic evidence demonstrates that ZNAs sensing is a regulatory function distinct from catalytic editing, suggesting that specifically blocking this domain could selectively activate innate immunity in tumors while preserving essential editing.

To date, there are a few emerging efforts focused on directly targeting the Zα domain either through drug repurposing or novel drug discovery approaches. Through high-throughput virtual screening of a list of FDA-approved drugs, Alendronate, Etidronate, and Zoledronate were identified as top candidate Zα binders following in silico modeling. 69 Despite these predictions, subsequent validation using NMR failed to detect their physical binding to Zα, and these compounds were therefore not advanced to cellular or in vivo evaluation. 117 However, Cromolyn, which appeared further down the screening list, was successfully shown to bind helix α3 of the ADAR1 Zα domain, which contains the critical residue Y177. Notably, NMR analysis confirms that Cromolyn did not bind the Zα domain of ZBP1, providing proof-of-concept that selective targeting of ADAR1-p150's Zα is feasible. Although limited cellular studies have examined its downstream effects, Cromolyn has not yet been evaluated in animal models. Its relatively weak binding affinity and lack of in vivo validation suggest that Cromolyn itself is unlikely to be therapeutically useful. Nevertheless, its core chromone moiety serves as a promising starting scaffold for further development of ADAR1 Zα inhibitors (Figure 2C). 117 Another high-throughput virtual screening effort identified natural compounds such as the Lithospermic acid and Regaloside B as potential Zα binders, with binding confirmed by surface plasmon resonance (SPR) (Figure 2C). 67 At the structural level, Lithospermic acid forms hydrogen bonds with Zα residues including H159, D160, and K169. Although these compounds passed the initial in silico Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, and Excretion (ADME) analysis, they currently lack robust cellular validation for their permeability and potency and therefore the functional consequences remain to be established. A more promising Zα-targeting effort is represented by AVA-ADR-001, which has progressed from cell-free biophysical binding studies to in vitro immune and tumor cell models, followed by evaluation in an immunocompetent syngeneic B16-F10 melanoma mouse model. 29‐31,68 AVA-ADR-001 has demonstrated good potency in “ISG-high” environments as a single agent and combination with anti–PD-1 therapy has shown promise in overcoming resistance in immune checkpoint–refractory melanoma models, consistent with earlier findings that ADAR1 loss promotes inflammatory reprogramming and enhances tumor immune recognition. 88 However, evidence of on-target engagement is limited to using indirect downstream functional readouts and detailed characterization of selectivity relative to another Zα-containing protein ZBP1 remains to be established, although it was found that highly tumorigenic cancer lines often has low levels of ZBP1. 71 Together, these efforts establish both the feasibility and challenges in targeting ADAR1-p150's Zα specifically. Nonetheless, these findings show that Zα-targeting has high therapeutic potential, as it may solve broad toxicity issue associated with global ADAR1 inhibition and the enhanced response in combination therapies remains an exciting avenue for continued investigation.

While direct Zα-targeting strategies remain in early development, modulation of ZNA conformations has emerged as an alternative approach to therapeutically engage the same biological axis. One such example is the small-molecule curaxin CBL0137, a DNA intercalator that promotes the B-to-Z DNA conformational transition and stabilizes left-handed Z-DNA (Figure 2C). 118 Through activation of ZBP1-dependent innate immune signaling and inflammatory cell-death pathways, CBL0137 enhances tumor immunogenicity and improves responses to immune checkpoint blockade in preclinical melanoma models. 119 Although CBL0137 does not directly inhibit ADAR1 or its Zα domain, its mechanism is conceptually relevant because ADAR1-p150 recognizes Z-form nucleic acids through its Zα domain and functions to restrain ZBP1-mediated innate immune activation. By increasing the abundance of Z-form nucleic acids and promoting ZBP1 signaling, CBL0137 may partially phenocopy the inflammatory consequences of impaired ADAR1 function. 119 Importantly, this therapeutic concept has progressed to clinical evaluation, with the ongoing Phase I MEL-212 trial (NCT05498792) investigating CBL0137 in combination with ipilimumab and nivolumab in patients with locally advanced or metastatic melanoma. Collectively, these findings highlight the translational potential of manipulating ZNA biology and further support the development of selective ADAR1-p150 Zα-targeting strategies.

sections.title: Assays-driven insights into ZNAs and Zα interactions

paragraphs.en: Functional assay-driven biophysical and cellular-based studies have substantially advanced our understanding of Zα interactions with ZNAs and small molecules. We hereby summarize the assays used to probe these interactions, which are critical for guiding the development of mechanistically selective ADAR1-p150 inhibitors.
Interactions between Zα and ZNAs

Biophysical assays (also known as cell-free binding assays), examine the direct in vitro interaction between target proteins and ligands. These assays enable detailed analysis of binding and structural dynamics between Zα and ZNAs (Table 1).

For example, the electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) and circular dichroism (CD) were used to confirm Zα preferential binding to Z-form nucleic acids, as exemplified by the band shift 120‐122 and reduced wavelength ellipticity of the nucleic acid upon addition of the recombinant Zα protein. 57 , 123 , 124

Additionally, isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) assays reveal that Zα stabilizes through multivalent binding and binding via helix-turn-helix (HTH) motif. 125 Exothermic ITC profiles could be used to imply on Zα:ZNA stoichiometry, 57 , 126 while distinct chemical shift perturbations shown in NMR can be used in mapping Zα binding sites and in characterizing the interaction dynamics with ZNAs. 53
Interactions between Zα and small molecules

Biophysical assays can also be used to shortlist potential inhibitors of Zα, to validate their actual binding performance with the computationally predicted binding affinity (Table 2). For instance, Kulkarni et al 31 identified AVA-ADR-001 as their first potential binder among nine other tested compounds as it demonstrated the highest thermal shift (2.5 °C) of the protein signal in the Thermal Shift Assay (TSA). In the same study, but using intrinsic tryptophan fluorescence (ITF) assay, titration of AVA-ADR-001 to Zα results in a strong Stern-Volmer quenching constant of (2.8 ± 0.07) × 104 M−1, suggesting strong binding affinity. 31 These findings help support the advancement of this compound to a further stage of drug development. Using SPR, the two repurposed compounds, Lithospermic acid and Regaloside B that were among the top predicted Zα-binders, exhibit equilibrium dissociation constants in the molar range: 7.56 × 10−5 M and 7.523 × 10−3 M, respectively. 67 These findings provide preliminary confidence to proceed with further evaluation of their inhibitory activity towards Zα. Similarly, Langdon et al 117 used microscale thermophoresis (MST) to assess cromolyn as a potential Zα inhibitor. MST titration indicated weak binding, with an estimated KD of 774 μM ± 301 μM. 117 Despite the modest affinity, the micromolar range KD at this early stage supports further exploration of the chromone scaffold.
Interactions between Zα and endogenous Z-nucleic acids

While cell-free binding studies provide structural insights, researchers utilize cell-based assays to bridge the gap between Zα-domain binding affinity and its functional role in stabilizing Z-conformations in the cells. These specialized cell-based assays (Table 3) could therefore inform on Zα functionality and could serve as useful tool to investigate and validate mechanism of action of the emerging Zα inhibitors. For instance, the immunofluorescence and RNA-immunoprecipitation sequencing (RIP-seq) studies using Z-RNA-recognizing Z22 antibody were pivotal in demonstrating that spliceosome inhibition triggers the accumulation of Z-RNAs from retained introns, triggering the ZBP1-induced necroptosis pathways in small cell lung cancer. 127

From spatial localization to genomic precision, researchers utilized Zα-based probes and/or ZNA antibodies for Chromatin Immunoprecipitation (ChIP) 124 , 128 and Chromatin Affinity Precipitation (ChAP) 120 studies to map regions of the human genome that are capable to adopt the ZNAs conformation. 120 , 128 Studies by Li et al 120 and Shin et al 128 proved that the Z-DNA forming regions are enriched along the transcription start sites, showing strong associations with actively transcribed genes and chromatin remodeling events. 120 , 128 This suggests that the Zα domain extends beyond a structural sensor of the Z-DNA but also as a stabilizing factor that facilitates the B-to-Z transition during transcription. 128 Although these assays are often utilized for genomic mapping, its readouts are fundamentally derived from a direct protein-DNA interface, where the Zα domain acts as a conformation-specific probe to bind with Z-DNA over B-DNA. 120 , 128 Consequently, the enrichment of specific DNA sequences indicates that the region has undergone a structural transition of Z-conformation. Further preservation through the formaldehyde crosslinking method in these assays stabilizes the otherwise transient Zα-Z-DNA binding, thereby enabling the capture of dynamic Z-conformations within a cellular context. 120 Despite the advancement of cell-based assays, a persistent challenge remains in capturing rapid, millisecond-scale dynamics of the B-to-Z transitions. Future research will require high-resolution live-cell reporters capable of visualizing Zα-ZNA interactions in real time. Given the recent findings of how oncogenic transcription factor like Myc is regulating Z-DNA transformation, delineating the exact mechanistic pathway of how Zα inhibition could lead to the lethal phenotype in cancer cells could fuel further drug development in this space.

Despite substantial advances in our understanding of ADAR1 biology, important questions remain regarding the cancer context–specific functions of the Zα domain and how its interactions with ZNAs contribute to therapeutic vulnerabilities. Most of the ADAR1-targeted compounds are still at the early pre-clinical stage (many confined to computational or cell-free systems validation) and present several challenges that limit their translational potential, including insufficient selectivity, increased toxicity associated with targeting constitutively expressed ADAR1-p110 isoform, and limited potency. Despite growing efforts in drug development, there remains a lack of predictive biomarkers to identify patients who are most likely to benefit from such therapies. Therefore, addressing current gaps to gain a deeper mechanistic understanding of ADAR1-Zα biology is essential to refine therapeutic strategies and enable more effective and targeted clinical applications.

ADAR1-p150 dependency has been observed in multiple cancers. 16 , 17 However, most studies rely on full ADAR1 depletion or catalytic mutants, making it difficult to distinguish Zα-dependent functions from canonical editing activity. In particular, the endogenous RNA substrates associated with Zα have not been clearly defined, limiting insight into both editing-dependent and potential editing-independent roles. Whether tumor dependency on ADAR1 is driven specifically by Zα-mediated functions, and whether this dependency mechanism is universal or context-specific across cancer types, remains to be determined.

Another major gap is the lack of a comprehensive mapping of ZNAs in tumors. Current understanding largely infers ZNAs formation from inverted repeat elements such as Alu sequences, 22 , 44 challenges remain in identifying the specific oncogenic or stress-induced transcripts that may preferentially adopt the Z-conformation, and finding out what thresholds of ZNAs accumulation could trigger those innate immune sensors. Addressing these gaps would enable systematic characterization of ZNA landscapes in tumors and help define the endogenous RNA substrates recognized by ADAR1 Zα, thereby clarifying how tumor-intrinsic conditions, including IFN signaling, regulate ZNAs formation and ADAR1-mediated immune suppression. Besides the indirect regulation of Zα domain on RNA editing, the functional consequences of the binding interactions between Zα and Z-DNA also remain to be elucidated.

While ADAR1-p150 has confirmative role in regulating IFN signaling and RNA sensing during viral infection, 130 , 131 the specific contribution of its Zα domain in anti-viral defense remains unclear. Addressing this gap could also clarify Zα function in virus-associated cancers, including those driven by human papilloma virus (HPV) and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). Taken together, to address the mechanistic gaps in cancer-specific contexts, future studies should focus on defining Zα-dependent mechanism using domain-specific models and determining whether tumor dependency on ADAR1-p150 is primarily mediated through ZNAs recognition, or a concerted effect of both ZNA recognition and deamination.

Although many mechanistic gaps remain, developing Zα-specific inhibitors that selectively target ADAR1-p150 offers a strategy to suppress tumor growth without significantly affecting the constitutively expressed ADAR1-p110 isoform in normal cells. From a translational perspective, the ADAR1–Zα–ZNAs axis is an underexplored yet promising therapeutic pathway. However, many potential ADAR1-Zα inhibitors are still in early phase of pre-clinical testing and yet to advance into human clinical trials. Meanwhile, systematic profiling of ADAR1-p150 expression in vital organs will be crucial to anticipate and mitigate systemic inflammation or other toxicities. Careful evaluation of context-specific mechanisms and monitoring normal tissue function will be essential for the development of safe and effective approaches to target ADAR1's Zα as an anti-cancer strategy. Continued integration of structural, biophysical and translational studies will be essential to define actionable biomarkers, sharpen mechanistic understanding, and guide the next generation of ADAR1-Zα-focused therapeutic strategies.
